transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. [Name]. Well, I'm here because... honestly, I just feel worn down almost all the time. It's this heavy, dragging feeling that just doesn't ever really go away. And the most frustrating part is that it doesn't even seem to matter how much rest I get. I can get a completely full night's sleep, you know, go to bed at a reasonable hour, do the whole wind-down routine, and I still wake up feeling just as exhausted as when my head hit the pillow. 

It’s been making my daily routine so difficult to manage. By the time I get through my workday—I work in the physical sciences, so it takes a lot of mental focus and just constantly being on top of the data—and then I come home and just look at the house... the clutter is just everywhere. Mail piling up on the kitchen counter, laundry sitting in the baskets, just things accumulating in every room. And by the time I've handled work and tried to even just make a tiny dent in that house clutter, I have absolutely very little left for anything else. I just have nothing left in the tank for myself. It's just this constant, unending tiredness that I can't seem to shake no matter what I do, and it takes so much out of me just to do the bare minimum of getting through the week, so I finally decided I needed to come in and talk to someone because I just can't keep running on empty like this every single day.
Have you noticed that you don’t enjoy things as much as you used to, or that you’ve lost interest in activities you used to find pleasurable?

Yeah, I think so. It’s not like I’m, you know, completely unable to function or anything like that. It’s more like... most days there’s just this low, gray mood that's constantly running in the background of my life. Like a hum you can't turn off. I mean, I still get up and go to the lab every day. I can still stand there and talk to my colleagues about the samples we're running or the data we're looking at, and I’m sure to them I seem perfectly fine, just going through the motions. 

But when it comes to the things I actually used to love doing just for myself... I just don’t feel that lightness anymore. I don't get excited. Like, I used to really love baking. I would spend my whole Sunday afternoon trying out new bread recipes or making these intricate little pastries, and I'd bring them into the lab on Monday for everyone. It was fun. But I haven't done that in so long. The thought of getting all the ingredients out and measuring everything and waiting for dough to rise... it just feels so flat. 

And my telescope, too. I have this really nice telescope set up in my backyard, and working in the physical sciences, you'd think I'd get enough of that at work, but I used to be out there for hours on clear nights. Just looking at the sky, tracking things, enjoying the quiet. It was my absolute favorite way to decompress. But lately, even if it’s a perfectly clear night with great visibility, I just look out the window and... I don't know, I just don't care. I don't have that spark to go out and check it the way I used to. It’s just this flat, gray feeling that sort of coats everything, if that makes sense? I just can't seem to find the joy in the things that used to actually make me feel like me.
How long have you been feeling this way, with that constant low mood and lack of interest in things you used to enjoy?

Well, if I really sit down and think about it, it’s been a while. It’s not like one day I just woke up and everything was suddenly gray, you know? It kind of crept in so slowly that I didn't even realize it was happening at first. But if I have to pinpoint a timeline, I'd say this... this low baseline, this feeling of just kind of existing rather than actually living, it’s been going on since shortly after we moved into our current house. 

It's an older house, lots of character, which we loved when we bought it, but it needed some work. We moved in a little over two years ago. I remember it was late spring, and the weather was just starting to get really nice, and we had all these grand plans for fixing up the yard and doing all these little renovations. And at first, I thought the tiredness and the lack of interest in my hobbies was just because of the stress of the move. Moving is exhausting, right? Everyone says that. You're packing boxes, dealing with real estate agents, changing your address on a million different things. So I just kept telling myself, "Oh, once we get unpacked, once we get settled, I'll get back to baking. I'll set up the telescope on the new patio." 

But then the boxes were unpacked, and the patio was set up, and... nothing changed. Months went by, and then a year went by, and then another year. And that feeling just stayed. It’s been a little over two years now of just feeling this way, every single day. I kept waiting for the fog to lift, thinking maybe it was the changing seasons, or a stressful project at the lab, or just the adjustment to the new commute. I would analyze it, you know, trying to find the variable that was causing the data to skew this way, because that's what I do, I look for reasons and patterns. But there wasn't a pattern, just this constant, steady, low-level hum of... I don't even know what to call it. Just not feeling like myself for over two years now. It's exhausting just thinking about how long it's been.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight over the past couple of years—like eating significantly more or less than usual or gaining or losing weight without trying?

No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. My appetite has been pretty much the same as it always is. I mean, I still eat my normal meals. My husband and I usually have dinner together when I get home from the lab, and I haven't noticed myself eating any more or less than I usually do. We tend to stick to a pretty standard rotation of meals, you know, chicken, vegetables, maybe some pasta. Sometimes we'll order takeout if I'm just too exhausted to even think about cooking, which, like I mentioned, happens a lot lately because of how drained I feel by the time I get through the door. 

But even when we get takeout, I just eat my normal portion. I don't find myself mindlessly snacking or, on the flip side, skipping meals because nothing sounds good. And as far as my weight goes, it's been completely stable. I have this scale in the bathroom, one of those digital ones that tracks everything, and I step on it maybe once a week or so, just out of habit. The numbers haven't fluctuated at all. My clothes still fit exactly the same as they did two years ago before we moved into this house. I have these work trousers that are pretty unforgiving if you gain or lose even a few pounds, and they still fit perfectly fine. So, yeah, no changes there at all. It's really just the exhaustion and that constant gray feeling, but my body itself, at least in terms of eating and weight, seems to be just chugging along exactly as it always has.
Have you noticed that you’re moving more slowly than usual, or that you can’t seem to sit still, maybe feeling restless or fidgety?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I haven't noticed anything like that. I know sometimes when people are stressed or anxious, they get that nervous energy, you know? Like they're tapping their foot constantly, or they can't stop playing with their pen, or they're just pacing around the room. My sister is like that. Whenever she's worried about something, she just can't sit still, she's always moving around, rearranging things, just generally being very fidgety. But I'm not like that at all. I don't have that restless feeling. 

And as for moving slowly... I mean, I'm tired, like I said. I feel drained a lot of the time. But I wouldn't say I'm physically moving slower. It's not like it takes me ten minutes to walk across the lab when it used to take two. I still get up, I walk to my car, I drive to work, I walk around the lab, I do my work... it's all at a normal pace, I think. I haven't had anyone ask me if I'm okay because I'm walking like a turtle or anything. It's more of an internal slowness, if that makes sense? Like my brain is just a little sluggish, or my motivation is dragging, but my physical body is still moving at its regular speed. 

I actually pay pretty close attention to things like that, being a scientist, you know, observing changes in behavior or physical state. And I haven't noticed any significant deviation from my baseline in terms of my motor functions or my energy levels in that specific way. I'm not bouncing off the walls, and I'm not moving through molasses. I'm just... moving normally, just with this heavy, gray cloud hanging over me while I do it. So, yeah, no restlessness and no physical slowness that I can tell.
Have you ever felt like you’re a failure or that you’ve let people down, or found yourself blaming yourself for things more than usual?

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I don't feel like a failure, and I don't think I'm letting anyone down. It's not really a feeling of guilt or blaming myself for things. I know sometimes people get really down on themselves and think everything is their fault, like if a project at work doesn't go perfectly, they think it's because they're incompetent or whatever. But I don't really do that. 

Like, at the lab, if an experiment doesn't yield the results we were expecting, I don't immediately think, "Oh, I messed this up, I'm a terrible scientist." I just look at the data and try to figure out what went wrong with the methodology or if there was an unforeseen variable. That's just how my brain works, I guess. I try to be objective about things. And even at home, with my husband, I don't feel like I'm failing him. He's been really understanding about how tired I've been. He knows I'm just not myself, and he doesn't make me feel guilty about not wanting to go out or not having the energy to do things on the weekends. 

I guess I just feel... empty, more than anything. It's not this heavy burden of guilt or feeling like I'm a disappointment. It's just a lack of feeling, a lack of joy. I don't sit around analyzing all my past mistakes or beating myself up over things I could have done differently. I just kind of get through the day, do my work, come home, and that's it. So, no, I don't have those feelings of being a failure or letting people down. It's just the tiredness and the grayness, really. I don't know if that makes sense, but it's just not a self-blame kind of thing for me.
Have you ever felt like life isn’t worth living or had thoughts about not wanting to be alive?

No, no, I haven't had any thoughts like that. I know that's something people worry about when you talk about feeling down for a long time, but that's really not where my head is at. I mean, I'm exhausted, yes, and I feel like I'm just going through the motions a lot of the time—waking up, going to the lab, coming home, eating dinner, going to sleep, and doing it all over again. It feels monotonous and gray, like I said, but I've never actually thought about not wanting to be here. 

I think part of it is just how my mind works. Being in the sciences, you get used to looking at things pragmatically. I can recognize that I'm not functioning at my best, that my mood is flat and my energy is low, but I still see the value in my life. I love my husband, even if I don't have the energy to do much with him right now, and I do care about my work, even if the passion for it feels a bit buried under all this fatigue. 

I've never sat there and thought, "I wish I wouldn't wake up tomorrow." It's more just... "I wish tomorrow wouldn't be so tiring." Or, "I wish I could just feel normal again." I don't want things to end; I just want them to feel different. I want that spark back. I remember reading once about how depression can make people feel completely hopeless, like there's no way out, but I don't feel hopeless. I just feel stuck in this rut. So, no, I've never considered anything like harming myself or feeling like life isn't worth it. I just want to figure out how to get through this gray patch and get my energy back so I can actually enjoy the life I have, you know?
Have you noticed a decrease in how much you get done during the day, either at work or at home, compared to how you used to function before this low mood started?

Well, yes and no. I mean, I'm still getting my lab work done. The daily experiments, the data collection, the things that have a strict protocol and a hard deadline—those are getting done. I show up, I do the physical work, I run the assays, I log the results. But... it's the other stuff. The stuff that requires more cognitive load, I guess you could say. Like, grant drafts. Writing grant proposals used to be something I could just sit down and power through over a few days, but now? It takes me noticeably longer. I stare at the screen, I write a paragraph, I delete it, I just can't seem to string the arguments together as efficiently. And even just routine project decisions—like deciding which variable to test next or how to adjust a methodology—it feels like my brain is wading through that molasses I mentioned earlier, even if my body isn't. It just takes more effort to process everything.

And then at home... that's where I think the decrease is more obvious, at least to me. I used to have a lot of hobbies that structured my downtime. I love baking, for instance. I used to bake fresh bread every weekend, trying different sourdough starters, experimenting with hydration levels—it's basically chemistry, right? But I haven't baked a loaf of bread in months. The thought of all the steps, the kneading, the waiting... it just feels exhausting. Same with my bonsai trees. I have a small collection that I used to meticulously prune and wire, but lately, I'm just doing the bare minimum to keep them alive. Watering them, mostly, but not the careful shaping they really need. 

And my telescope! I have a really nice Dobsonian telescope, and I used to plan these whole evenings around astronomical events, mapping out which constellations or planets I wanted to observe. I'd bundle up, take it out to the backyard, spend hours out there. But now... it's just gathering dust in the corner of the living room. I look at it, and I think, "I should take that out tonight, the sky is clear," but then I just sit on the couch instead. So, yeah, I'm functioning, I'm keeping my job, I'm paying the bills, but the actual *amount* of things I'm getting done, especially the things that used to bring me a sense of accomplishment or joy... that's definitely decreased. It's like my capacity has shrunk, and I'm only doing what's absolutely necessary to keep the baseline going.
Have you noticed that even small tasks, like making your bed or taking a shower, feel unusually tiring or require a lot more effort than they used to?

Oh, absolutely. It’s funny you mention taking a shower, because that’s actually one of the things I’ve really noticed lately. I used to just hop in, wash my hair, get out, you know, a quick ten-minute thing in the morning. But now... I’ll just stand there under the hot water for I don't know how long, just dreading the physical effort it’s going to take to actually lather the shampoo, rinse it out, and then dry myself off. It sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud, because it's literally just a shower, but it feels monumental. 

And making the bed is the same way. Half the time I just sort of pull the duvet up haphazardly and leave the pillows wherever they landed, because taking the extra two minutes to tuck the sheets in just feels like climbing a mountain. 

I’m really here because I feel worn down almost all the time. It’s this deep, heavy tiredness that just doesn't ever seem to lift. And the frustrating part is that it doesn't even matter how much I rest. Like, I'll get a full night's sleep—I make sure I'm in bed by a reasonable hour, I sleep through the night, but when the alarm goes off, I don't feel refreshed in the slightest. I wake up feeling like I ran a marathon in my sleep. 

So I have to drag myself out of bed, force myself through that exhausting shower, and go to the lab. And by the time I’ve handled work for the day, and then come home and tried to tackle just the basic house clutter... I mean, there's always clutter, right? The mail piling up on the kitchen island, the coffee cups left by the sink, the laundry that needs to be moved from the washer to the dryer. I try to keep on top of it because my husband is already being so patient with me and I don't want the house to turn into a complete disaster zone. But honestly, by the time I’ve pushed through my job and sorted out that baseline level of house clutter, I have very little left for anything else. 

The tank is just completely empty. That's why the telescope stays in the corner and the bonsai trees don't get trimmed. The energy just isn't there for anything beyond the absolute bare minimum of getting through the day. It’s just a constant, relentless exhaustion, no matter what I do.
Would you say that your mood is depressed most of the day, nearly every day, rather than just feeling tired or drained?

That’s a really interesting way to put it, because I’ve actually spent a lot of time trying to untangle that exact thing in my own head. You know, is it just the physical exhaustion, or is it something else? And I think... well, I’d have to say it is more than just being drained. Most days, nearly every day, really, there’s this low, gray mood just constantly running in the background of everything I do. It’s like a hum that never turns off. 

I mean, I can still go to the lab, obviously, and I can stand there at the bench and talk to people. I can chat with my colleagues about the experiments or whatever administrative gossip is going around the department that week, and I’m totally capable of having a normal conversation and smiling when I’m supposed to. I can go through the motions of interacting. But underneath all of that, I just don’t feel... light. I don't feel that spark. It’s like someone turned the saturation down on my whole life. 

I think about the things that used to make me really excited, like my baking—you know, getting a perfect rise on a new sourdough recipe and pulling it out of the oven—or taking the telescope out on a crisp, clear night to look at Jupiter's moons. I used to get this genuine thrill, this real sense of anticipation and joy just thinking about doing those things. And now, even when I try to picture doing them, that feeling is just completely absent. It's just flat. 

So, yes, it’s definitely more than just my body being tired. It’s this persistent, overcast feeling in my mind that just hangs there, day in and day out. It doesn't even seem to matter if it's a busy Tuesday at the lab or a quiet Sunday on the couch, that grayness is just always there, making everything feel completely muted. I keep waiting to wake up and feel that old enthusiasm, to feel like myself again, but the mood just sort of blankets everything.
Have there been times when your mood or energy level got so bad that you felt you needed more help than you were getting, like maybe needing to take time off work or seeing someone sooner?

No, no, it’s never really been like a... a crisis, if that makes sense. I haven't ever called in sick because of my mood, or felt like I needed to rush to an emergency appointment or anything dramatic like that. It's more of a slow burn, you know? 

Like I was saying before, I’m still functioning. I still go to the lab every single day. I mean, in physical science, especially with the kind of data collection I do, if you just don't show up, the whole experiment could be completely ruined. The assays I run, they have very specific, rigid timelines, and if I’m not there to add the reagents at exactly the right hour, or if I miss logging the temperature changes, literally weeks of work just go down the drain. So taking time off... honestly, it almost stresses me out more to think about taking time off than it does to just drag myself in and do the work. 

My husband, bless him, he sometimes looks at me in the morning when I'm just standing there staring blankly at the coffee maker, and he'll say, "Why don't you just use a sick day?" But I just can't. I always push through. It’s never gotten to a point where I completely break down or physically cannot get out of bed at all. It's just that getting out of bed feels like I'm carrying a hundred-pound weight on my shoulders. 

So, no, I haven't felt like I needed urgent help or a leave of absence or anything severe like that, because I always manage to do what absolutely has to be done. It's just that doing it takes absolutely everything I have, every ounce of my willpower, and there's nothing left for me at the end of the day. But the baseline? The baseline always gets met. I always manage to show up.
Have you ever found yourself feeling worthless or like you’re not measuring up, even when things seem objectively fine?

Well, I mean... no, not really. I wouldn't use the word worthless, no. It’s actually kind of funny, because you’d think with how tired I am and how much I struggle with just the basic stuff lately, that I would feel like a failure, but I really don't. I know I'm competent. 

Like at the lab, for instance, I know my assays are incredibly precise. I've been doing this kind of data collection for a long time, and my principal investigator completely trusts my work. I never look at my results or my career and think, "Oh, I'm terrible at this," or "I'm not measuring up to everyone else." I know exactly how good I am at what I do. 

And even at home, with the house stuff and the clutter I mentioned... I know I'm not a bad person or, you know, a worthless wife just because there are coffee cups by the sink or because I didn't have the energy to fold the laundry right away. My husband is always telling me how much he appreciates me, and I know he genuinely means it. I don't sit there and beat myself up or feel like I don't deserve him or my job. It's really not a self-esteem issue at all. 

Like, just last week, we had this big departmental meeting, and I had to present some of my recent findings. And objectively, I knew the data was rock solid. I stood up there, I gave the presentation, I answered all the committee's questions perfectly fine. I didn't feel like an imposter or anything like that. I knew I belonged there and that my work was valuable. But the whole time, I was just so profoundly drained. 

So it's not that I feel like I'm failing or that I'm not enough... I just feel like succeeding takes way, way too much out of me. The competence is there, the self-worth is there, it's just the energy and the... the color that's missing. So, no, I don't really struggle with feeling worthless.
Have you noticed that you get more easily annoyed or irritated lately, even by small things that wouldn’t have bothered you before?

Honestly... no. I don't think I have the energy to be irritated, if I'm being completely honest. It’s actually kind of the opposite. You know, to be annoyed by something, you have to actually care enough about it to let it get under your skin, and you need a certain amount of energy to feel frustrated. 

Like, just on Tuesday, one of the undergrads in the lab, who is very sweet but sometimes a bit careless, accidentally knocked over a rack of pipettes that I had just finished organizing for a very specific assay series. A couple of years ago, I would have been so annoyed. I wouldn't have yelled, obviously, but I would have felt that sharp spike of frustration, you know? That feeling of being exasperated because I had just finished setting all of that up. But this time? I just looked at the plastic rolling across the bench and felt... nothing. Just this heavy realization that I was going to have to bend down and pick them up. 

My husband even noticed it at home. He accidentally shrank one of my favorite sweaters in the wash last weekend, and he came to me looking so apologetic, bracing himself for me to be upset. And I just looked at the tiny sweater and thought well, I guess I just do not wear that anymore. It wasn't even a blip on my radar emotionally. I didn't care at all. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I'm irritable or getting annoyed by small things. If anything, things that probably should bother me just sort of bounce off this gray wall I was talking about earlier. It takes a certain spark to get angry, and I just don't have it. It is just way too exhausting to be mad.
Have you noticed that it's harder to focus or think clearly lately, like you're having trouble concentrating on your work or making decisions that used to feel simple?

Well, yes, actually. That... that is something I've noticed, and it's been incredibly frustrating. It's not like I'm completely forgetting things or, you know, losing chunks of time, but it's just... it's like my brain is wading through molasses. Everything just feels so much slower than it used to. 

Like, at work, I do a lot of writing—grant proposals, literature reviews, that sort of thing. And it used to be that I could sit down, look at a paragraph I needed to revise, and I could just see the structure, you know? It was clean, it was sequential. I'd know exactly which sentence needed to move where, which transition was clunky, and I'd just fix it and move on. But lately, I will literally sit there staring at the same four sentences for twenty minutes. I'll rewrite a sentence, and then I'll look at it, and I'll think, "Wait, is that better? Does that even make sense?" And I'll second-guess myself over and over on the most basic phrasing. A paragraph that should take me five minutes to polish is suddenly taking me half an hour because my thoughts just aren't sharp anymore. 

And it's not just the high-level science stuff, either. It bleeds into everything. My husband and I are doing some minor repairs on the house—nothing major, just fixing up the guest bathroom—and we needed to pick out a new faucet and some drawer pulls. A year ago, I would have walked into the hardware store, looked at the options, said, "Okay, brushed nickel, clean lines, that one," and been out in ten minutes. But we went last weekend, and I stood in that aisle looking at, I don't know, fifty different brushed nickel faucets, and I just could not make a decision. My brain was just spinning its wheels. I kept thinking, "Well, this one has a slightly higher arc, but this one matches the towel rack better, but what if the handle on this one feels weird?" It was paralyzing. I ended up just telling my husband to pick one because I literally could not process the information well enough to make a choice. 

So, yes, the concentration and the decision-making... it's definitely taken a hit. It's like I have to work twice as hard just to think half as clearly, and it makes everything—whether it's a grant revision or buying hardware—feel like this massive, insurmountable task.
Would you say that your depressed mood has been present for most of the day, more days than not, for the entire two years you've been feeling this way?

Well, yes, if I really sit down and map it out, that's exactly it. It’s practically every day. It’s just this constant... low baseline. And as for the timeline, yes, it’s been the entire two years. 

Actually, it started right around the time my husband and I moved into our current house. It’s this older house, which we loved because it has all this original character, you know? The mature trees in the yard, the solid wood floors. We closed on it, and I remember the first few weeks were just your standard, run-of-the-mill moving stress—unpacking boxes, figuring out where the furniture should go, setting up the utilities. But then, shortly after we moved into the older house—a little over two years ago now—that's when I really noticed this shift. This heavy, gray baseline just kind of settled over me. 

And it hasn't really lifted since. So it's been a little over two years now of just waking up and feeling like the color is turned down on my life. It's not like I have these long stretches where I'm perfectly fine and energized for a month and then down again. It’s just... there. Every morning when I make my coffee, every afternoon when I'm running assays at the lab, every evening when I'm sitting on the couch in that older house we bought. It’s just this persistent, quiet drain in the background of everything I do. 

So, yes, to answer your question, it is definitely more days than not, and usually the whole day. I kept thinking, you know, maybe it was just the adjustment to the new commute, or getting used to the quirks and the maintenance of an older home, or just the dust from unpacking. I kept waiting to bounce back to my normal self. But the boxes got unpacked, the seasons changed, a whole two years passed, and this low baseline just stayed. So, yes, it's been most of the day, nearly every day, for that entire time.
Have you noticed that you no longer get pleasure or satisfaction from things that used to make you happy, even things you really enjoyed doing?

You know, actually... I’ve thought about this kind of thing, and no. I wouldn't say that. I still really enjoy the things I’ve always liked. It’s just that I’m, well, tired, like I was saying before, but the actual feeling of satisfaction? That’s still completely intact. 

For example, I’ve been cultivating this indoor garden for years. Mostly orchids—Phalaenopsis, a few Dendrobiums. And they are incredibly finicky, especially in this older house because the draftiness can really mess with the ambient humidity, and the windows don't have the same UV filtering as newer panes. So I have this whole setup in the sunroom with a humidifier and specific grow lights that I calibrated myself to make sure they're getting the exact right spectrum. And just this past Sunday, I was out there checking the root systems—because you have to be really careful about root rot, especially when you use a sphagnum moss mix instead of just straight orchid bark—and I saw that one of my oldest orchids, the one I actually brought home from my very first lab job years ago, was pushing out a new flower spike. 

And I honestly felt... really happy. I felt that genuine little thrill of excitement. I sat there for probably an hour just misting the leaves and wiping them down with a little diluted neem oil, just enjoying the quiet and the satisfaction of seeing something thrive because I took the time to care for it properly. My husband even came in with coffee and we just sat there looking at the new growth. I really loved it. 

And I still love cooking, too. I made this incredibly complicated beef bourguignon a couple of weeks ago. It took all afternoon, you know, taking the time to pat the chuck roast completely dry, searing the meat in small batches so it wouldn't steam in its own juices, reducing the burgundy wine, making sure the pearl onions were perfectly caramelized... the whole nine yards. It’s a lot of steps, and like I said, my focus isn't great right now, so it took me longer than it should have. But when we finally sat down to eat it, it was absolutely delicious, and I felt really proud of it. I enjoyed every single bite, and we even had a glass of wine with it, and it was just a really nice evening. 

So, no, the joy isn't gone. I still like the things I like, and I still get that spark of satisfaction when a recipe turns out right or a plant blooms or when I read a really good chapter in a book. It's just that the baseline underneath it all, the rest of the time, is that heavy, gray feeling. But the actual pleasure in my hobbies and the things I love? No, I haven't lost that at all.
Would you say that you experience less pleasure or satisfaction from activities overall, even if you still enjoy them when you do them?

No, I really wouldn't say that either. I know I mentioned earlier that my baseline feels like the color is turned down on my life, but when I'm actually doing the things I enjoy, the volume on that specific joy hasn't been turned down at all. The pleasure is just as bright and full as it ever was. 

Like when I was talking about that beef bourguignon? The satisfaction I got from tasting that sauce after it had finally reduced for three hours... it wasn't a muted satisfaction. It wasn't like, "Oh, this is okay, I guess." It was exactly the same level of culinary triumph I would have felt five years ago, long before this whole heavy, gray cloud settled in over everything else. 

And it’s the exact same thing with my orchids. When I saw that new flower spike last Sunday, it wasn't just a fleeting, watered-down kind of happiness. It was a deep, resonant feeling of accomplishment. Because, like I said, orchids are incredibly temperamental, especially the Phalaenopsis in a drafty older house. You can do absolutely everything right—the ambient humidity, the weak weekly fertilizer schedule, the light cycle—and they still might just decide to drop all their buds because the temperature in the room fluctuated two degrees in the wrong direction overnight. So when you actually get one to push out a new spike, it's a real victory. And I felt that victory completely. 

It wasn't lessened or diluted by the fact that I've been feeling so drained lately. The drain is definitely there when I'm just existing, you know? When I'm waking up, or driving to the lab, or just sitting around the house trying to figure out what to do next.
